title: The Interwar Period and Unresolved Tensions
subject: AP World History
objectives: Analyze the political and economic instability of the interwar period, including the failures of the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression
Explain the rise of authoritarian and totalitarian regimes (fascism in Italy and Germany, militarism in Japan, communism in the USSR)
Compare fascism and communism as responses to the crises of the interwar years
Describe how unresolved tensions from World War I led toward a second global conflict

sections.heading: A Wheelbarrow of Money for a Loaf of Bread
sections.content:
In the German city of Berlin in late 1923, a woman went to buy bread and brought her money in a wheelbarrow — not because she was wealthy, but because the German mark had become almost worthless. Prices were doubling every few days. A loaf of bread that cost a couple of marks before the war cost hundreds of billions of marks by November 1923. People papered their walls with banknotes because the paper was cheaper than wallpaper, and workers were paid twice a day so they could rush to spend their wages before the money lost value by evening. A lifetime of savings could be wiped out in a week. This was hyperinflation, and it was just one of the disasters that battered the world in the two decades between the two great wars.

The period from 1919 to 1939 is called the INTERWAR PERIOD, and its central theme is INSTABILITY. World War I had not resolved the world's tensions; in many ways it had deepened them. The peace was bitter, economies were shattered, and millions of people had lost faith in the old political order — in democracy, in capitalism, in the promises of their leaders. Into this vacuum of fear and disappointment stepped a new and terrifying kind of political movement, promising order, glory, and revenge.

This lesson explains how the unresolved tensions of World War I, made far worse by a global economic catastrophe, gave rise to brutal authoritarian and totalitarian regimes — fascism in Italy and Germany, militarism in Japan, and communism in the Soviet Union. Understanding the interwar period is understanding the CAUSES of World War II. The story of why the second war happened begins not in 1939 but in the wreckage of the first.

sections.heading: Instability: Versailles and the Great Depression
sections.content:
Two great sources of instability dominated the interwar years. The first was the failure of the post-WWI PEACE. The Treaty of Versailles had left a poisonous legacy, especially in Germany, where people seethed at the 'war guilt' clause, the crushing reparations, the lost territory, and the gutted military. Germans spoke of being 'stabbed in the back,' and that humiliation and resentment became raw material for extremist politicians. The LEAGUE OF NATIONS, the international organization created by the peace to prevent future wars, was fatally weak: the United States never joined, it had no army of its own, and it could only recommend, not enforce. When aggression came, the League proved unable to stop it.

The second and even more powerful source of instability was the GREAT DEPRESSION. After a fragile recovery in the 1920s, the U.S. stock market crashed in October 1929, and because the global economy was deeply interconnected — with American loans propping up Europe — the collapse spread worldwide. International trade shrank, banks failed, factories closed, and unemployment soared to staggering levels: roughly a quarter of American workers and a third of German workers were jobless at the depths of the crisis. The Depression discredited the existing capitalist, democratic order. If the system could collapse like this, throwing millions into poverty, then perhaps the system itself was the problem — a conclusion that made radical alternatives, both on the far right and the far left, suddenly attractive to desperate people.

Here is the crucial causal point for the exam: economic catastrophe is political dynamite. Frightened, impoverished, humiliated populations became willing to trade freedom for the promise of bread, order, and national pride. The Depression did not by itself create fascism or militarism, but it supplied the desperation that those movements fed on. The tinder of WWI's unresolved grievances was set ablaze by the spark of economic collapse.

sections.question: How did the Great Depression contribute to the rise of authoritarian regimes in the 1930s?
options: It made everyone wealthy, so they demanded stronger governments
Mass unemployment and economic collapse discredited the existing democratic, capitalist order and made desperate populations receptive to radical movements promising order, jobs, and national pride
It only affected the United States and had no global political impact
It strengthened the League of Nations and prevented dictatorship
sections.explanation: The Depression spread worldwide through the interconnected economy, causing mass unemployment (about a quarter of U.S. and a third of German workers) and discrediting democracy and capitalism. Desperate, frightened populations became willing to trade freedom for radical movements promising bread, order, and national glory — fueling fascism and militarism.

sections.heading: The Rise of Totalitarianism: Fascism, Militarism, Communism
sections.content:
Out of this crisis emerged regimes that concentrated power and controlled society to a degree never before possible — made possible by the same industrial, bureaucratic, and propaganda tools that total war had pioneered. Historians call the most extreme of them TOTALITARIAN: states that sought total control over politics, the economy, culture, information, and even the private beliefs of their citizens, typically under a single party and a charismatic leader, enforced by secret police, propaganda, and terror.

FASCISM was the new ideology of the radical right. It was ultra-nationalist, glorified the state, the nation, and the leader above the individual, celebrated military strength and violence, and defined itself fiercely against both democracy and communism. In ITALY, Benito Mussolini, exploiting postwar chaos and fear of communism, took power in 1922 and built the first fascist state. In GERMANY, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party rose on the back of Depression-era misery and Versailles resentment, came to power legally in 1933, and then dismantled democracy. Nazism added a core of vicious, genocidal RACISM and antisemitism, blaming Jews and others for Germany's humiliations and promising racial 'purification' and the conquest of 'living space' (Lebensraum) in the east. In JAPAN, the Depression strengthened ultranationalist MILITARISTS who increasingly dominated a nominally constitutional government, glorified the emperor and army, and pursued imperial expansion in Asia as the solution to Japan's economic and resource problems.

On the radical left stood COMMUNISM in the Soviet Union. Born of the Russian Revolution, the USSR under Joseph Stalin became a different kind of totalitarian state, built on a Marxist promise of a classless society. Stalin forced rapid industrialization through Five-Year Plans, COLLECTIVIZED agriculture (causing famines that killed millions, including in Ukraine), and unleashed the Great Purges, executing or imprisoning millions of supposed enemies. Fascism and communism were bitter ideological enemies, yet as forms of government they shared striking features — one-party dictatorship, state control, secret police, propaganda, and the crushing of individual freedom — a comparison the AP exam loves to test.

sections.heading: Interwar Authoritarian Regimes Compared
rows: First fascist state; glorified state and leader
Dismantled democracy; rearmed; Lebensraum; persecuted Jews
Army dominance; imperial expansion in Asia

sections.content: The unresolved tensions of World War I — a bitter peace and a weak League of Nations — combined with the Great Depression to discredit democracy and produce totalitarian regimes: fascism in Italy and Germany, militarism in Japan, and communism in the USSR.
sections.heading: Core Takeaway

sections.question: Fascism and Soviet communism were bitter ideological enemies, yet as FORMS OF GOVERNMENT they shared which key features?
options: Free elections, multiple political parties, and a free press
One-party dictatorship, state control of society, secret police, propaganda, and the suppression of individual freedom
A commitment to liberal democracy and capitalism
Complete government non-involvement in the economy
sections.explanation: Despite being ideological opposites (radical right vs. radical left), fascist and communist states were both totalitarian: one-party dictatorships that controlled the economy and society, used secret police and propaganda, and crushed individual freedom and dissent. The AP exam frequently tests this structural comparison.

sections.heading: Reading the Rise of Hitler as a Historian
sections.content:
Let's trace the causation chain behind Hitler's rise the way an AP essay should, connecting long-term and immediate causes. In the early 1920s, Hitler and the Nazis were a fringe movement; Hitler even landed in prison after a failed 1923 coup. During the relatively stable, prosperous mid-1920s, the Nazis won almost no votes. What changed everything was the GREAT DEPRESSION. As unemployment exploded after 1929, Nazi votes surged in tandem — desperate Germans turned to a movement that promised jobs, national revival, and someone to blame.

Now layer the causes. The LONG-TERM cause was the resentment bred by the Treaty of Versailles, which Hitler relentlessly exploited, promising to tear it up and restore German greatness. The IMMEDIATE economic trigger was the Depression, which turned that latent resentment into mass support. And the SYSTEMIC weakness was a fragile, discredited democracy whose squabbling parties could not govern the crisis, leading conservative elites to hand Hitler the chancellorship in 1933 in the mistaken belief they could control him. Once in power, he moved with terrifying speed to outlaw other parties, crush opposition, and establish a totalitarian dictatorship.

Notice the analytical structure: Versailles resentment (long-term grievance) + the Great Depression (economic trigger) + weak democratic institutions (enabling condition) + Hitler's exploitation of all three (agency) = the Nazi seizure of power. This is exactly how a strong causation answer works — not a single cause, but a layered, interacting set of causes that together explain an outcome. Hold onto this structure; it is the reasoning skill the entire unit is building toward, and you will use the very same chain to explain the outbreak of World War II.

steps.title: Choose meaningful categories of comparison
steps.content: Don't compare randomly. Pick categories that matter — for fascism vs. communism, compare ideology (right vs. left, nationalist vs. class-based), economic policy, methods of control, and view of the individual. Good categories make a comparison analytical rather than a list of facts.

steps.title: Identify specific similarities
steps.content: State precise shared features: both were one-party dictatorships, used secret police and propaganda, controlled the economy and information, and crushed individual freedom. 'Both were bad' is not analysis; 'both used a single party and secret police to suppress dissent' is.

steps.title: Identify specific differences
steps.content: Name concrete contrasts: fascism glorified nation and race and preserved private property under state direction, while communism aimed at a classless society and abolished private ownership of the means of production. Specific differences show real understanding, not vague generalities.

steps.title: Make an argument about the comparison
steps.content: Top comparison answers go beyond similarities and differences to argue a point — e.g., 'Although fascism and communism were ideological opposites, both arose from the same interwar crises and adopted strikingly similar totalitarian methods.' A thesis that explains the comparison earns the complexity point.

sections.heading: Don't Blur Fascism, Communism, and 'Authoritarian'
sections.content: Precision matters here and the exam punishes sloppiness. (1) FASCISM is a radical-RIGHT, ultranationalist ideology (Italy, Nazi Germany); COMMUNISM is a radical-LEFT, class-based ideology (USSR). Calling Hitler a communist or Stalin a fascist is a serious error. (2) They were bitter ENEMIES ideologically but shared totalitarian METHODS — keep the 'enemies in ideology, similar in structure' distinction straight. (3) NAZISM is a specific form of fascism with genocidal racism/antisemitism at its core — don't treat all fascism as identical to Nazism. (4) Do NOT skip the GREAT DEPRESSION when explaining the rise of these regimes; it is the central economic cause and a favorite of causation prompts. (5) Remember the LEAGUE OF NATIONS was weak and that the U.S. never joined — a common factual slip.

sections.heading: Frame the Interwar Period as Causes of WWII
sections.content: On the exam, treat the interwar period as the CAUSE side of a causation question about World War II. Keep a ready chain: WWI's bitter peace (Versailles) + a weak League of Nations + the Great Depression → the rise of fascist/militarist regimes (Hitler, Mussolini, Japanese militarists) bent on aggressive expansion → WWII. For a comparison prompt, compare fascism and communism (ideological opposites, structurally similar totalitarian states) or compare the responses of different governments to the Great Depression. Always anchor claims in SPECIFIC evidence — 'reparations and the war-guilt clause,' 'a third of German workers unemployed' — rather than vague references to 'problems.'

sections.heading: Interwar Period Essentials
sections.content: INSTABILITY (1919–1939). PEACE FAILURE: TREATY OF VERSAILLES resentment in Germany (war guilt, reparations, 'stabbed in the back'); a weak LEAGUE OF NATIONS (no U.S., no army, could not enforce). GERMAN HYPERINFLATION (1923). GREAT DEPRESSION: U.S. stock crash 1929 spreads worldwide through the interconnected economy → mass unemployment (~25% U.S., ~33% Germany) → discredits democracy/capitalism. TOTALITARIAN REGIMES: FASCISM (radical right, ultranationalist) — MUSSOLINI (Italy, 1922), HITLER/Nazis (Germany, 1933; + racism/antisemitism, Lebensraum); MILITARISM (Japan — army dominance, imperial expansion); COMMUNISM (USSR — STALIN: Five-Year Plans, collectivization + famine, Great Purges). KEY COMPARISON: fascism vs. communism = ideological OPPOSITES but structurally similar TOTALITARIAN states (one-party, secret police, propaganda, no individual freedom). These unresolved tensions = the CAUSES of WWII.

sections.heading: Why the Interwar Crisis Still Speaks to Us
sections.content:
The interwar period is one of the most studied and most cautionary chapters in all of modern history, because it shows how quickly a modern, educated, industrialized society can abandon democracy under the pressure of fear and economic pain. Germany in the 1920s was one of the most advanced, cultured nations on earth, with a functioning democracy. Within a few years of the Depression, it had handed absolute power to a movement built on hatred and grievance. That trajectory — from democracy to dictatorship by way of economic crisis, wounded national pride, and the search for scapegoats — has haunted political thinkers ever since, and it is why economists and historians watch economic crises so anxiously for their political consequences.

The period also reveals deep continuities with the rest of your course. The totalitarian state was made possible by the very tools of industrial modernity you have studied: mass propaganda through new media (radio, film), bureaucratic organization, the mobilizational techniques pioneered in WWI's total war, and the modern state's vastly expanded reach into citizens' lives. Nazism's genocidal racism, as you saw in Unit 6, drew on the scientific racism and social Darwinism that imperialism had normalized. And Stalin's forced industrialization was, in a sense, a brutal communist answer to the same question the whole world faced after Unit 5 — how does a society industrialize and catch up? — answered through state terror rather than markets.

For the exam, this lesson is the indispensable bridge between the two world wars, and it is built to develop two reasoning skills at once. It runs the unit's core skill of CAUSATION forward — the interwar crises are the causes of WWII — and it introduces COMPARISON (fascism vs. communism, different governments' responses to the Depression), a skill you will need across the course. When you reach the next lesson on the causes of World War II, you will find that you have already learned them here: a vengeful, rearming Germany, an expansionist Japan, a feeble League, and democracies too exhausted and distracted by economic crisis to stop the gathering storm.
